nameStory: Common peppergrass gets its spicy name from its tiny seeds, which have a sharp, peppery bite when crushed between your teeth. Early settlers and Indigenous peoples used these zesty little seeds as a seasoning, much like we use black pepper today. The 'grass' part of the name comes from its weedy, lawn-like growth habit that spreads across disturbed ground.
description: Common peppergrass is a small, weedy annual that rarely grows taller than your knee, usually reaching just 6-18 inches high. This scrappy member of the mustard family has a bushy, branched appearance with tiny white flowers clustered at the tips of its many stems. The whole plant has a somewhat fuzzy, grayish-green look and tends to grow in patches across disturbed soil. Despite its humble appearance, it's incredibly common and can pop up almost anywhere people have disturbed the ground.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, round, flattened seed pods (called silicles) that feel papery and make a soft rattling sound when shaken. Each pod is about the size of a pinhead and contains seeds with a sharp, peppery taste that will make your tongue tingle.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Minuscule white flowers with four tiny petals, clustered in dense, elongated spikes at branch tips. The flowers are so small you might need to look closely to see the individual petals, and they have a faint, slightly sweet smell.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are deeply toothed or lobed with a slightly fuzzy texture, while upper leaves become narrower and less divided. The leaves feel somewhat rough and have a mild peppery taste when chewed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a bushy, much-branched plant that spreads outward from the base, creating dense patches. The stems feel slightly rough and are often tinged with red or purple, especially near the base.

habitat: Common peppergrass thrives in disturbed soils and can be found along roadsides, in parking lots, garden edges, and waste areas throughout New England. It particularly loves compacted, poor soils where other plants struggle to grow. You'll often spot it growing alongside other weedy mustards in sunny, open areas from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of deeply lobed leaves that taste distinctly peppery when nibbled. Plants begin their rapid growth phase as soil warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs with tiny white flower clusters appearing at branch tips, quickly followed by the development of characteristic round seed pods. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Mature plants turn brown and papery, with seed pods rattling in the wind. The dried plants often persist, making identification possible through the tiny round pods.
seasonality.winter: Dried, skeletal remains may persist through early winter, with empty seed pods still clinging to brittle stems, though most plants have dispersed their seeds and decomposed.

funFact: Common peppergrass seeds were so valued as a pepper substitute during colonial times that some settlers specifically encouraged it to grow in their kitchen gardens, making it one of the few weeds that was actually cultivated as a spice crop in early New England.
confusionNotes: Common peppergrass is easily confused with its cousin Virginia pepperweed, but common peppergrass has distinctly hairy, grayish foliage while Virginia pepperweed appears smoother and greener. Memory trick: 'Common is fuzzy, Virginia is smooth.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'grass,' this plant is actually in the mustard family and completely unrelated to true grasses. The mustard family connection becomes clear when you taste the peppery leaves or seeds, which contain similar compounds to horseradish and mustard.
compareHints: Among the pepperweeds in New England, common peppergrass stands out for its notably hairy, grayish appearance and densely packed seed clusters. Virginia pepperweed is much smoother and greener, while field peppergrass has distinctly heart-shaped seed pods rather than round ones. The fuzzy, dense growth habit of common peppergrass makes it look almost silvery from a distance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Virginia pepperweed differs from its peppergrass cousins mainly in its seed pods and leaves.
Among the pepperweeds, field peppergrass stands out with its forking flower branches and arrow-shaped stem leaves that clasp without leaf stalks.

Broadleaved pepperweed stands out from its pepperweed relatives by being much taller (3-6 feet vs 1-2 feet), having wider leaves, and forming large perennial colonies rather than growing as individual annual plants.
Unlike its upright pepperweed relatives like Virginia pepperweed and field peppergrass, lesser swine-cress grows in flat mats rather than standing erect.
Smith's cress differs from its peppergrass relatives by having distinctly different leaf shapes on the same plant - deeply cut lower leaves and smooth upper ones.
Unlike Virginia pepperweed and field peppergrass which have similar leaves throughout the plant, clasping pepperweed has dramatically different leaf shapes from bottom to top.
Among its pepperwort relatives, narrow-leaved pepperwort stands out for having the thinnest, most finely divided leaves - much more thread-like than Virginia pepperweed or field peppergrass.
